newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-HK lawyers face new Chinese-language era.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK lawyers face new Chinese-language era.

text.p: Hong Kong's lawyers and judges are facing the toughest case of their careers -- digesting 21,000 pages of British legalese translated into modern Chinese.
That's a brief of several million Chinese characters -- to be absorbed ahead of the British colony's return to Chinese rule on July 1.
Among the territory's top judges and barristers are still some expatriate Westerners who have little or no Chinese-language skills.
Can such members of the legal community adapt to the language of a new era?
The jury is also out for some Chinese lawyers whose main working language is English.

Most courts in the colony are a mirror image of Britain's ancient legal system, where robed, bewigged barristers and judges address each other with elaborate titles such as "learned counsel" and "my lord".
So far, in the mostly-Chinese territory, the major court exchanges remain in English, even if Chinese people are involved, leading to a laborious interpretation process during trials.
Obscure English words in the territory's laws have forced translators to invent new legalese in Chinese for Hong Kong's justice system, complicating the learning process for some lawyers.
A nine-year translation job has included the creation of a special legal dictionary.
COURTS SCRAMBLE TO MEET JULY DEADLINE
As 156 years of British colonial rule ends in Hong Kong at midnight on June 30, the courts themselves will have to remain law-abiding by being ready to use the Chinese language.
"Come July 1, if Hong Kong courts cannot take on cases in Chinese we will be contravening the Basic Law," Alice Tai, Judicial Administrator, told Reuters.

The Basic Law is the constitution China has established for the territory after July 1. As civil servants scurry to complete myriad details of the translation, politicians worry that the transformation in the legal system could weaken Hong Kong's legal framework and threaten business confidence.

"There seems to be some movement, out of political correctness, that we should become as Chinese as we possibly can with the legal system, and get rid of judges who are not Chinese ....all these developments would be bad for the system," said Margaret Ng, a legislator and lawyer.
THE DELICATE QUESTION OF WORDING

"The (English) Common Law is well established, but this system is expressed through some peculiar terminology where neither the concepts nor the words exist in Chinese," government law draftsman Tony Yen said.
This was particularly true of land inheritance, laws which have descended from the feudal system of the English Middle Ages.

"We had to coin new words," Yen said. This upset lawyers who had to struggle with the new Chinese vocabulary. Hong Kong jurists want their proven system to go on working in the new era. They are uneasily aware that China, which has promised a "hands-off" attitude, has a grim reputation for summary justice, with show-trials and swift punishment including frequent executions.

Critics expressed relief that a reform-minded and bilingual lawyer Andrew Li was named Chief Justice of China's future Special Administrative Region, believing this bodes well for Hong Kong's cherished judicial independence.

Privately, civil servants say they are optimistic about China's approach to law in Hong Kong, though pro-democracy activists and Western countries are uncomfortable about planned moves to curb civil liberties after the handover.
"It would be fair to say China has developed a hell of a lot in the past 10 to 15 years in terms of its legal framework, (but) the problem is enforcement," a top bureaucrat said.
